## Modal mixture, or a system of its own?

Some textbooks explain blues as **modal mixture**: chords borrowed from major, minor and the
modes into one key. Hein's test case is Booker T. & the M.G.'s *Green Onions* (1962). Its riff
uses three chords per bar, and each chord comes from a different mode of the key.

In the grid, each coloured dot names a mode of the key note that holds every note of that chord.
Press play and watch the colours change from bar to bar.

<div class="bz" data-w="onions" data-title="The Green Onions riff: where each chord comes from"></div>

Hein's chords for the three riff positions are Fm7 – A♭ – B♭, B♭7 – D♭ – E♭ and C7 – E♭ – F
(in F). The bars here are laid out as a standard 12-bar, and the riff's rhythm is simplified.
Check both against the recording.

The I-position chords all fit F Dorian. D♭ needs F natural minor. C7 and F major need F major.
Hein argues that "mixture" assumes major and minor are separate worlds that get mixed. In a
blues they were never separate. Of John Lee Hooker's *I'm Bad Like Jesse James* he says there
is no way to tell which mode is the native one, so the song is simply "in E blues".

## Cross harp: playing an instrument against its design

A diatonic harmonica is built for the major key of its name. Blowing gives the key chord, and
drawing (breathing in) gives a dominant 9th chord on the 5th. Hein describes how Black players
reversed this, starting around 1870-1920. In **cross harp** (2nd position) the draw chord
becomes the home chord, the blow chord becomes IV, and bending the draw notes down gives the
blue notes. Van der Merwe calls it perhaps the most striking example in all music of
technique contradicting an instrument's design.

<div class="bz" data-w="harp" data-title="Ten-hole harmonica (Richter layout)"></div>

The hole layout and bends shown are the standard Richter tuning, written from memory and
**not yet checked** against a source. Overblows are left out.

## The 12-bar form: neither needed nor enough

The 12-bar is a **scheme**, not a definition. Hein's examples of 12-bar forms that are not
blues are Flatt and Scruggs's *Shuckin' the Corn* (bluegrass) and the 1966 *Batman* theme.
His examples of blues without the 12-bar are *Work Song* (Nat Adderley) and *Moanin'* (Bobby
Timmons). For the form itself, see [Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar
Blues](blues-changes.qmd), and train your ear on it with [Blues Changes by
Ear](../practice/blues-ear.qmd).

## Blues tonality in other styles

The later part of Hein's essay looks at how much blues tonality a style uses. Funk uses a lot
(*Jungle Boogie*: one chord, blues pitch). Disco uses much less. Aretha Franklin's *Bridge Over
Troubled Water* brings blues tonality into a song that is diatonic in Simon and Garfunkel's
original. Hein closes with a case for teaching blues tonality in the core theory course, and
for keeping it in school arrangements, which often strip it out and add V–I cadences.

These examples come from a summary of the second half of the essay, not a word-for-word
reading, so they are **unverified** here until the essay is re-read.

**Try it:** take a song you know in major. Set the backing to **One chord: I7** and play its
melody with majorish 3rds and high 7ths. What has to change for it to sound like blues?
